items.readable_text:
Content:
Suppose we want to calculate [MATH: \lim_\limits{x \to \infty} x^2] and [MATH: \lim_\limits{x \to -\infty} x^2.] To do this, we can use the graph of [MATH: y=x^2,] which takes the familiar shape of a parabola.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/bb0b4dd9154debe346e257fc87059532]

Content:
On the right side of the graph, we see that [MATH: y] increases without bound as [MATH: x \to \infty.] On the left side of the graph, we have a similar situation: [MATH: y] again increases without bound as [MATH: x \to -\infty.] Consequently, we have

Content:
[MATH: \lim_\limits{x \to \infty} x^2=\infty\qquad \textrm{and}\qquad \lim_\limits{x \to -\infty} x^2=\infty.]

Content:
Notice that the functions [MATH: y=x^4] and [MATH: y=x^6] have a similar shape, and as such their limiting behavior is the same.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/afc9e9d1d4cf97b908b4b97887c1fad8]

Content:
In general, whenever [MATH: n] is an even natural number, we have

Content:
[MATH: \lim_\limits{x \to \infty} x^n=\infty\qquad \textrm{and}\qquad \lim_\limits{x \to -\infty} x^n=\infty, \qquad \textrm{for}\qquad n=2,4,6,\ldots.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The graph [MATH: y=x^{12}] looks similar to an upward parabola, so

[MATH: \lim_\limits{x \to \infty} x^{12} = \infty .]

However, multiplying by the negative coefficient [MATH: -12] causes [MATH: y=-12x^{12}] to look more like a downward parabola. This changes the sign of the limit. Therefore,

[MATH: lim_(x → ∞)(− 12x^{12}) = − lim_(x → ∞)(x^{12}) = − ∞.]

Content:
To compute the limit at infinity of a general polynomial, we only need to consider the term with the largest exponent, called the leading term. All of the other terms can be disregarded!

Content:
For example, to compute [MATH: \lim_\limits{x\to \infty} \left( 6x + 2x^3-7x^2+12\right) \, ,] we identify the leading term and compute its limit. Here, the leading term is [MATH: {\color{blue}{2x^3}},] so we have

Content:
[MATH: lim_(x → ∞)(6x + 2x^{3} − 7x^{2} + 12)|= lim_(x → ∞)(2x^{3}); = lim_(x → ∞)(x^{3}); = ∞.]

Content:
The reason this works is that when [MATH: x] becomes very large, the behavior of the polynomial is dominated by the term with the largest exponent.

Content:
Watch out! The leading term is not always the first term that appears in the expression. Rather, it is the term with the largest exponent. This term may appear anywhere in the expression.

Content:
The reason why we call the term with the largest exponent the "leading" term is that when the polynomial is arranged in standard form (with exponents ordered from greatest to least), the term with the largest exponent appears first:
[MATH: 6x+ {\color{blue}{2x^3}}-7x^2+12 \quad \to \quad {\color{blue}{2x^3}}-7x^2+6x+12]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Suppose we want to calculate [MATH: \lim_\limits{x \to \infty} x^2] and [MATH: \lim_\limits{x \to -\infty} x^2.] To do this, we can use the graph of [MATH: y=x^2,] which takes the familiar shape of a parabola.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/bb0b4dd9154debe346e257fc87059532]

Content:
On the right side of the graph, we see that [MATH: y] increases without bound as [MATH: x \to \infty.] On the left side of the graph, we have a similar situation: [MATH: y] again increases without bound as [MATH: x \to -\infty.] Consequently, we have

Content:
[MATH: \lim_\limits{x \to \infty} x^2=\infty\qquad \textrm{and}\qquad \lim_\limits{x \to -\infty} x^2=\infty.]

Content:
Notice that the functions [MATH: y=x^4] and [MATH: y=x^6] have a similar shape, and as such their limiting behavior is the same.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/afc9e9d1d4cf97b908b4b97887c1fad8]

Content:
In general, whenever [MATH: n] is an even natural number, we have

Content:
[MATH: \lim_\limits{x \to \infty} x^n=\infty\qquad \textrm{and}\qquad \lim_\limits{x \to -\infty} x^n=\infty, \qquad \textrm{for}\qquad n=2,4,6,\ldots.]

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: The Effect of Coefficients

Content:
Multiplication of a power function by any positive real constant does not influence its limit at infinity. For example,

Content:
[MATH: lim_(x → ∞)2x^{2}|= lim_(x → ∞)x^{2} = ∞]

Content:
because [MATH: y=2x^2] is an upward parabola, just like [MATH: y=x^2.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/76185aa4a61b4811f227bc51cf486318]

Content:
On the other hand, multiplication of a power function by a negative real constant changes the sign of the limit. For example,

Content:
[MATH: lim_(x → ∞) − 2x^{2} = − lim_(x → ∞)x^{2} = − ∞]

Content:
because [MATH: y=-2x^2] is a downwards parabola that points in the opposite direction as [MATH: y=x^2.]

---

Item 3 — Example: Computing the Limit at Infinity of a Power Function With an Even Power

Example Prompt:
Find [MATH: \lim_\limits{x \to \infty} \left(-12x^{12}\right).]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The graph [MATH: y=x^{12}] looks similar to an upward parabola, so

[MATH: \lim_\limits{x \to \infty} x^{12} = \infty .]

However, multiplying by the negative coefficient [MATH: -12] causes [MATH: y=-12x^{12}] to look more like a downward parabola. This changes the sign of the limit. Therefore,

[MATH: lim_(x → ∞)(− 12x^{12}) = − lim_(x → ∞)(x^{12}) = − ∞.]

Item 6 — Tutorial: Computing the Limit at Infinity of a Power Function With an Odd Power

Content:
Now let's look at the graph of [MATH: y=x^3.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/0f414490f46b606844c43d9005b8e909]

Content:
We notice that the situation here is different:
[MATH: \lim_{x \to \infty} x^3=\infty \qquad\text{and}\qquad \lim_{x \to -\infty} x^3=-\infty.]

Content:
These limits are valid for any power function of the form [MATH: x^n,] where [MATH: n] is an odd natural number.

Content:
[MATH: \lim_\limits{x \to \infty} x^n=\infty\qquad \textrm{and}\qquad \lim_\limits{x \to -\infty} x^n=-\infty, \qquad n=1,3,5,\ldots.]

Content:
Again, multiplication of [MATH: x^n] by a positive constant does not affect the limit at infinity. However, multiplication by a negative constant changes the sign of the limit.

---

Item 7 — Example: Computing the Limit at Infinity of a Power Function With an Odd Power

Example Prompt:
Evaluate [MATH: \lim_\limits{x \rightarrow -\infty} \dfrac{x^3}{2}.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, we note that

[MATH: lim_(x → − ∞)(x^{3})/(2)|= lim_(x → − ∞)((1)/(2) ⋅ x^{3}); = (1)/(2) ⋅ lim_(x → − ∞)x^{3}.]

The graph [MATH: y=x^3] is power function with an odd positive power and therefore has the property that

[MATH: \lim_{x\to-\infty } x^3 = -\infty.]

Multiplication by the positive constant [MATH: \dfrac{1}{2}] does not affect the limit at infinity. So, we have

[MATH: (1)/(2) ⋅ lim_(x → − ∞)x^{3}|= lim_(x → − ∞)x^{3}; = − ∞.]

Item 10 — Tutorial: Infinite Limits of Constant Functions

Content:
Constants do not vary with [MATH: x.] So, any limit of a constant evaluates to just the constant itself.

Content:
For example, we have
[MATH: \lim_\limits{x \to \infty} 3=3.]

Content:
Likewise,

Content:
[MATH: \lim_\limits{x \to -\infty} \sqrt{ \pi}= \sqrt{\pi} .]

Content:
In general, for any constant [MATH: C,] we have

Content:
[MATH: \lim_\limits{x \to \pm\infty} C=C.]

---

Item 11 — Example: Computing the Limit at Infinity of a Constant Function

Example Prompt:
Given that [MATH: p(x)=9x^4] and [MATH: q(x)=3x^4], what is [MATH: \lim_\limits{x \to -\infty} \dfrac{p(x)}{q(x)}?]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
When we divide the two functions, we get a constant, and the limit of a constant is just the constant itself:

[MATH: lim_(x → − ∞)(p(x))/(q(x))|= lim_(x → − ∞)(9x^{4})/(3x^{4}); = lim_(x → − ∞)3; = 3]

Item 14 — Tutorial: Limits at Infinity of General Polynomials

Content:
To compute the limit at infinity of a general polynomial, we only need to consider the term with the largest exponent, called the leading term. All of the other terms can be disregarded!

Content:
For example, to compute [MATH: \lim_\limits{x\to \infty} \left( 6x + 2x^3-7x^2+12\right) \, ,] we identify the leading term and compute its limit. Here, the leading term is [MATH: {\color{blue}{2x^3}},] so we have

Content:
[MATH: lim_(x → ∞)(6x + 2x^{3} − 7x^{2} + 12)|= lim_(x → ∞)(2x^{3}); = lim_(x → ∞)(x^{3}); = ∞.]

Content:
The reason this works is that when [MATH: x] becomes very large, the behavior of the polynomial is dominated by the term with the largest exponent.

Content:
Watch out! The leading term is not always the first term that appears in the expression. Rather, it is the term with the largest exponent. This term may appear anywhere in the expression.

Content:
The reason why we call the term with the largest exponent the "leading" term is that when the polynomial is arranged in standard form (with exponents ordered from greatest to least), the term with the largest exponent appears first:
[MATH: 6x+ {\color{blue}{2x^3}}-7x^2+12 \quad \to \quad {\color{blue}{2x^3}}-7x^2+6x+12]

---

Item 15 — Example: Computing the Limit at Infinity of a General Polynomial

Example Prompt:
Calculate [MATH: \lim_\limits{y\rightarrow -\infty} (44-3y^4-9y^{12}) \, .]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We identify the leading term and compute its limit:

[MATH: lim_(y → − ∞)(44 − 3y^{4}− 9y^{12})|= lim_(y → − ∞)(− 9y^{12}); = − lim_(y → − ∞)(y^{12}); = − ∞]
